source: A magnet has a north pole and a south pole. Opposite poles attract and like poles repel. Magnets pull on iron and steel, but not on wood, plastic, paper, glass or most coins.
Thinking magnets attract every metal. Iron and steel stick; aluminum foil, copper and gold do not.
A fridge magnet holds up a drawing. A compass needle points north. Both are magnets.
Every magnet has a north pole (N) and a south pole (S). Opposite poles attract (N and S pull together). Like poles repel (N and N, or S and S, push apart).
Flip a magnet to see the poles attract or repel.

Magnets pull on things made of iron or steel (and a few other metals, like nickel). They do not pull on wood, plastic, paper, glass, aluminum, copper or gold. The pull works through paper and even through your hand.
Sort the things: does a magnet pull them?
The north pole of one magnet faces the north pole of another. What happens?
Both facing poles are N: like poles.
Thinking magnets attract all metals. Foil, pennies and soda cans (aluminum) do not stick.
The Earth itself is a giant magnet. A compass needle is a small magnet that turns to line up with it, so its north end points north.
Going further. William Gilbert showed in 1600 that the Earth is a magnet: Gilbert: On the Loadstone. Later: Magnets in Physical Science.
